Researchers asked participants three questions: whether they believed most people could be trusted, whether someone would take advantage of them if given the chance, and whether people are generally helpful or selfish in their choices.

While the results for all three indicated declining trust, the most dramatic decrease was in belief that others can be trusted, Biddle said.

He also noted that trust remains strongest among "older Australians, degree holders and the employed".

The findings follow data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics’ General Social Survey from 2025 that found half of Australians felt others could be trusted — compared to 61 per cent in 2020.

Similarly, Scanlon Foundation Research Institute CEO Anthea Hancocks said the findings reflected those of her organisation.

"People who are employed each day or very often are going to a workplace where there are other people working towards a similar goal — and they're getting paid," she explained.

"That gives you a greater sense of self-worth that you may not necessarily have if you're unemployed."

She suggested that higher trust among older Australians may be related to her organisation's findings that this cohort had "a higher sense of belonging than any other age group".

"That's generally because they know the world in which they're living; they're quite comfortable with their circumstances," she said.

"They know what they are and have an understanding of what the future holds. Unlike young people, whose sense of belonging is way below average."

The ANUpoll also found that between March and June of 2026, life satisfaction in Australia plateaued at 6.22 out of 10.

Over the same period, the proportion of those who experienced difficult or very difficult levels of financial stress decreased slightly from 34.9 per cent in March to 33 per cent in June.

body.en:
Ashleigh Middleton has spent months campaigning to keep a drug that's holding her cancer at bay on Australian shelves.

Now she's won — but says the uncertainty surrounding long-term access hasn't gone away.

The 31-year-old breast cancer patient was shocked when it was announced in April that Zoladex — a monthly implant used to suppress hormones in women with hormone-positive breast cancer as well as a range of other conditions affecting women — would be pulled from the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) and no longer supplied through its usual distribution pathway from 1 November.

The decision, made by the drug's manufacturer, AstraZeneca, prompted concern among patients and clinicians who questioned how those who rely on the treatment would access an alternative and whether suitable substitutes would be available for all conditions the implant is used to treat.

title.en: What is Garma Festival? Australia's biggest Indigenous gathering returns for 2026
title.zh: 什么是加尔马节？澳大利亚最大的原住民聚会将于2026年回归

summary.en: The annual Garma Festival, Australia's largest Indigenous gathering, is set to return this weekend on Yolŋu Country, celebrating Indigenous culture.
summary.zh: 澳大利亚最大的原住民聚会——一年一度的加尔马节将于本周末在约尔古地区举行，庆祝原住民文化。

body.en:
Thousands of people will travel to north-east Arnhem Land this week as the Garma Festival returns to Yolŋu Country for four days of ceremony, culture and national conversation.

Held on Gumatj Country in the Northern Territory, Garma remains Australia's largest Indigenous cultural gathering .

This year marks more than a quarter of a century since it started as a small community gathering, and will run from 31 July until 3 August.

Each year it brings together Yolŋu Elders, artists, young people, political leaders, academics, business representatives and visitors from across the country.

It is a place where ancient ceremony sits alongside some of Australia's biggest conversations about First Nations policy.

This year, those discussions will unfold without Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, despite his commitment last year to attend every Garma while serving as prime minister.

Hosted by the Yothu Yindi Foundation since 1999, Garma was established to celebrate and strengthen Yolŋu culture while creating a place where Aboriginal knowledge, leadership and ideas could be shared with the broader Australian community.

The word Garma comes from Yolŋu Matha and refers to a meeting place where different ideas come together through a process of two-way learning.

That philosophy remains central to the festival today. While Garma is grounded in Yolŋu ceremony and tradition, it has also become one of Australia's most influential forums for discussion on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander affairs.

Each year, governments, community organisations, academics and industry leaders travel to Arnhem Land to listen, learn and engage directly with Yolŋu leaders on Country.

Garma is held at Gulkula, a sacred ceremonial site on Gumatj Country near Nhulunbuy in north-east Arnhem Land.

Surrounded by stringybark forest and overlooking the Gulf of Carpentaria, Gulkula has been a place of ceremony and renewal for generations.

According to Yolŋu tradition, it is where the ancestor Ganbulapula introduced the yidaki into Yolŋu life, making it one of the region's most culturally significant places.

Unlike many conferences, Garma is held on Yolŋu Country and led on Yolŋu terms.

Rather than Aboriginal leaders travelling to Canberra, governments, institutions and organisations travel to Arnhem Land, placing First Nations culture, knowledge and authority at the centre of the national conversation.

Visitors camp on Country throughout the four-day festival and are asked to observe cultural protocols guided by their Yolŋu hosts.
